title: Relative contributions of personality, psychosocial functioning, and executive cognition to individual differences in delay discounting.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Delay discounting (DD) is a widely studied individual-difference phenotype that reflects preferences between smaller immediate and larger delayed rewards. Previous studies have linked DD to demographic characteristics, personality traits, psychosocial functioning, and cognitive abilities. However, the relative incremental contribution of these domains within the same predictive framework remains unclear.
METHODS: We analyzed data from 1,193 healthy young adults from the Human Connectome Project-Young Adult dataset. Delay discounting was indexed by the area under the discounting curve for the $200 condition. Participants were randomly divided into a training set (= 953) and a hold-out test set (= 240). Hierarchical models sequentially incorporated demographic variables, personality and psychosocial measures, and executive cognitive measures. Ordinary linear regression, Elastic Net, and XGBoost were evaluated using apparent training performance, nested five-fold cross-validation, and hold-out testing. Model performance was assessed using the coefficient of determination (), Root-mean-square error (RMSE), and Mean Absolute Error (MAE). Incremental value was quantified as the change inbetween adjacent models (Δ).
RESULTS: Age and gender alone had little predictive value for DD. In the primary hierarchical models, the largest initial improvement occurred after personality and psychosocial measures were added, with a further increase after cognitive measures were included. The cognition-first analysis, however, showed that cognitive predictors produced similar gains when entered directly after the demographic baseline, particularly with Elastic Net and XGBoost. Thus, the apparent difference between the two predictor domains depended partly on the order in which they were entered. XGBoost fit the training data substantially better than the linear models, but this advantage largely disappeared under cross-validation. In the hold-out test set, Elastic Net performed best (= 0.0507, RMSE = 0.1976, MAE = 0.1522), although overall prediction remained modest. An expanded sensitivity analysis using 257 available non-imaging predictors likewise showed low validated predictive performance.
CONCLUSIONS: Personality-psychosocial and cognitive measures both provided incremental predictive information beyond demographics, although their apparent relative contributions varied with predictor-block order. However, the modest validated performance indicates that delay discounting is influenced by multiple factors beyond those captured by the present models. These findings support a multidomain perspective on individual differences in delay discounting while highlighting the importance of cautious interpretation of predictive performance in large-scale behavioral datasets.
